title: How to pick the best flat when you can't go back
description:
With 20 viewings and a yes-or-no on the spot, a gut-feel pick gets you the very best flat 1 time in 20 (5%). Instead, view the first 7 and turn them all down, then sign the first flat that beats all 7: you end up with the very best 38% of the time, and a top-3 flat 63% of the time. The catch: if the best was among the first 7 (35% of the time) nothing beats it and you're left with the last one. The rule scales: skip the first 37% of any list and you still get the best about 37% (1/e) of the time. Mathematicians call it the secretary problem; Martin Gardner published it in Scientific American in 1960.

Numbers checked in code (exact formula plus 1,000,000 simulated flat hunts). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_problem

facts_checked: Random pick of 20 gets the best: 1 in 20 = 5% (verify.py)
Best cutoff for 20 options: skip 7 (20/e = 7.4); chance of the very best 38.4% exact, 38% in 1,000,000 simulated hunts (verify.py)
Skip 7 of 20: a top-3 flat 63% (simulated); random pick top-3: 15% (verify.py)
Best is among the first 7: 7/20 = 35%, then nothing beats the bar and you take the last (verify.py)

Optimal rule: reject the first ~n/e, then take the first better than all seen; success -> 1/e; first published by Martin Gardner, Scientific American, Feb 1960 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_problem)

beats.say: Take the first nice flat, and you'll miss the best.
But waiting for perfect is worse. Say no, and someone else signs it. No going back.
You've got 20 viewings this month. Each one is yes or no, on the spot.
Pick on gut feel, and your odds of getting the very best are one in 20. 5%.
So, step one. View the first 7, and say no to all of them. Even the great one.
You're not picking yet. You're learning what good looks like.
Step two. From flat 8 on, sign the first one that beats all 7.
Now you get the very best flat 38% of the time, not 5. And a top 3 flat, nearly two times in three.
The catch: if the best was in your first 7, nothing beats it, and you're stuck with the last one. That's 35% of the time.
But it scales. 100 flats? Skip 37. A thousand? Skip 368. Either way, you land the very best 37% of the time.
